utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The witness will be coming in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth continues to apply. And Mr. Djurdjic is to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at Exhibit P836.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, we are going to see now the Byrnes-Djordjevic Agreement dated the 25th of October, 1998. You will agree that this agreement governs the check-points and observation points and the location where police forces are going to be deployed. But let's start from the beginning. Below the list of the check-points, you will agree that it has been left open for this issue to be considered by the 29th of October, 1998; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will also agree that under item 2, it is envisaged that in the case of incidents, the police can patrol in armoured vehicles and use machine-guns up to 7.9 millimetre, and in self-defence and with maximum restraint?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move now to item 3. We see here that from certain places, the stationary forces are to withdraw; is that correct? Whereas they are going to remain in Malisevo, Orahovac, Zociste, Restane, Suva Reka and Dulje?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you agree with me that there is no mention at all about the number of forces in the places where the police is allowed to stay?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in my mind the most important part is this last part, probably you are familiar with it, but I suspect the Chamber isn't. We see here that the Orahovac-Suva Reka road is mentioned and that the traffic on that road will be regulated in the coming 15 days?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me how many kilometres are there between Orahovac and Suva Reka? Roughly speaking, I know that you can't give me the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is Kosovo Trivial Pursuit. I would need a map. I'm sorry, I'm not going to speculate. I need a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't want you to guess. What I wanted to tell you -- we are talking about the Orahovac Suva-Reka road on which the police is not allowed to patrol according to this agreement; is that correct? For 15 days.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along the Suva Reka road, correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But they are allowed to travel from Orahovac to Malisevo via Suva Reka then Dulje and then again to Malisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think the Court would benefit from a map on this. Have we got a map?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think we do. If you will bear with me until I find the number of the exhibit. We'll get back to this; I have to save time. I'll show it to you later. So after the expiry of this 15-day period, the police was allowed to travel directly from Orahovac to Malisevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you from your opinion. What do you think -- why was this provision is inserted banning the police to travel over the 15 days from Malisevo to Orahovac, in whose interest and benefit was this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two aspects to this I think. One was that there were a lot of displaced people in the hills hiding, and the other was that the KLA were given time to extract themselves. I don't know which of those two is more important, but certainly the issue of needing to allow displaced people to go back to their homes without harassment was certainly one of the factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us that the police were barricaded the whole time at the police station in Malisevo with sand bags and that they only ventured out in order to do their patrols in armoured vehicles; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, then how did the police pose a threat to the population if the situation is as I've just described it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people that -- the people in the area that we talked to firmly stated that they were -- they felt very intimidated by the police, the police presence, which they considered to be excessive. I don't know how many patrols -- how many vehicles patrolled at a time, but that was the impression we got, and that was why we approached the issue of recommending that for everyone's sake in order to calm the situation, that that police presence should be -- should make it itself look less threatening. And one of the ways it could do that was reducing the size of the presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind the reports from your verifiers and your daily reports, KVM was constantly being escorted by this police patrolling between Malisevo and Suva Reka?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not constantly being escorted. I think the KVM had freedom of movement to go where it felt it needed to. I think sometimes the police were on the road at the same time and sometimes they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit D156, please. I do not need the B/C/S version on the screen. Can we just provide an English version for the witness and enlarge it so that he can read it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at item 1. First paragraph of item 1. Will you agree that during the verification conducted on the 5th of January, 1999, it was noted that: "Not all the OPs were manned. Full details of the verification are contained in the individual regional centre daily reports."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When this verification was conducted, you did not establish that the agreement had been breached?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's wrong. We did establish that the agreement had been breached because elsewhere it has been shown that we reported that the the majority of the 27 OPs were occupied. So this proves that -- that not more than 26 were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Based on the report of the 6th and after the verification, it just says that not all were occupied whereas no specific number of how many were indeed occupied was given; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but elsewhere you will recall that we reported that the majority of the 27 were occupied. And since the key number was nine, the majority is more than nine. Considerably more than nine. So I don't have the exact number, I'm very sorry. If I had had that piece of paper, I would have rendered it back in 2000 or 2002 or 2006. I don't have it, but I'm convinced in my mind that there were a lot more than nine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, did you see a protest letter if you sent one to the Yugoslav authorities regarding the occupation of a larger number of the OPs than the one envisaged in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was reported to Vienna and I -- on a report, and I verbally reported this to General Loncar in one of the regular liaison meetings at which MUP liaison were present. I'm sure it was also discussed separately between the officer who was responsible for MUP liaison and his MUP counterpart. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the document that you are talking about in the course of all the proceedings in which you appear has never been shown to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document are we talking about, please? I've -- I have several.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Any document addressed to Loncar or anyone else --

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not a document given to Loncar. It was a verbal statement given to Loncar face to face by me and I recall those meetings vividly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So we are just talking about verbal exchanges, we are not talking about documents. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to 65 ter document 00636.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, we are going now to look at a table in which breaches are specified and listed. It starts with a preamble containing the description of what constitutes breaches and what were operational breaches and then we see the table. If I understood correctly, sir, those were the reports that you occasionally sent to the Security Council and to Vienna?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a compendium of all of the previously reported breaches, but bringing them together systematically in one document. Because the chairman in office was in the process of doing a periodic report to the UN and wanted this as one document rather than trying to extract it from all of the daily reports. That was the purpose of this document. And it was put together by the -- the three people that worked in Walker's office putting the daily reports together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the first page of the table, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, here we have a legend. This white square means FRY non-compliance, the black one means KLA non-compliance, and the last one half black and half white diagonally is non-attributable.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to go through all the incidents, I'm just going to highlight a few of them. Please look at a January 20th on this first page. It says: "In Racav the village was surrounded by a MUP force of 8 to 10 vehicles, three brothers, a doctor, and two teachers, were eventually arrested for weapons possession." And we see that there's a white rectangle here, white square, which means that this indicates an FRY non-compliance.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in accordance with paragraph 6 of the UN Security Council resolution and further on with whatever number 4 was. So if you go back to the front of the document where the different paragraphs of the UN Security Council resolution are listed, then you can find out what -- the reason why that was considered to be non-compliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So therefore you think that the FRY authorities should not have arrested persons for illegal possession of weapons pursuant to Resolution 1199?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which was issued by the head of mission, under the head of mission's authority, and it was his -- this document would have gone to him and they'd have gone through all of the incidents, and they would have said why they felt that that was a non-compliance. It was probably harassment, and it was probably the fact that they may have been arrested and were never charged and did not go through due process. I don't know. But that is my -- that's my suspicion in this case. And since we are all speculating, that's my speculation. But I certainly can't remember every individual case of the many hundreds that we listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, this is a document that you have provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to the next page now, please. No, no, no, please, the next page after this one. I can't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please look at the entry dated 29th January. It reads: "25 Kosovo Albanians and one Serb policeman were killed in the village of Rogovo, midway between..." et cetera. And this was again attributed to the FRY forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got this. I think I can help you with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Arresting terrorists in possession of illegal weapons and -- by refusing to surrender, and we even have a report that a policeman was attacked and a rifle was snatched from him, all of these incidents are attributable to the FRY; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, we are looking at the 29th of January, are we, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on the 29th of January, Serb Special Forces storm an Albanian farm where they suspect it is a safe house for KLA transiting. I believe that they carried out -- and that was entirely legitimate. I believe they carried out a good operation until the moment having gone over the wall, there having been an exchange of fire, one Serb policeman having been killed, a number of the Albanians having been killed but not all of them. At that point the Albanians surrender. At that point it stops being a legitimate police operation because at that point the police load the Albanians into their minibus, lock the doors, and then riddle it with bullets and kill all of them in cold blood without any judicial process taking place. That is why that is non-compliance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the source for everything that you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of that is partly the impressions of my people who were there before me and partly, I believe, the testimony of the one survivor of this who hid under a haystack and subsequently told his story to us. I don't have those documents, but I'm giving you my recollection of things as I recall them ten years later. And I fully understand that I'm under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you see the documents that you are referring to? Have they been shown to you in the course of these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The written report of the verifiers who were there before me, I have seen and I have handed in in the course of the previous -- the previous meetings with the ICTY staff. The testimony of the survivor was not seen by me; but I understand it was taken, and it was handed to UN authorities, which would have been probably in the course of February 1999. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, in the chronology you prepared with the most important dates included, you noted for the 29th it's probably a safe house of the KLA but not all of them were armed. When you were making this in 1999, you did not note this, nor did you do so in May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What did I not note?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I've just read to you the entry, the location is probably a KLA safe house but probably not all of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stand by that. It was probably a safe house for the KLA. They were -- a few of them were in uniform, most of them were not. We were told -- I was told that all were armed. I was shown 12 weapons. No forensic examination was carried out on those weapons to see whether those weapons were linked with the deceased. They could just as easily have been from the back of the MUP van and placed at the scene of the crime. So I wrote there the facts that I understood, that it was a KLA safe house, that they were probably KLA transiting. The people that were the owners of the farm may or may not have been KLA because they may well have been pressured into offering their safe house. No identification of who were the -- who were the people who originally lived there who may have well have been put under pressure, and the people who may more not have been KLA in civilian clothes. I never saw any attempt to differentiate them. They were all just thrown in the same heap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you seek from the Yugoslav authorities an on-site investigation report because an on-site investigation judge was there to investigate and there were other forensic and ballistic reports as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good, I'm glad you mentioned that. There was a so-called investigation by the judge. It appeared to take about two hours. And in two hours you cannot investigate a scene of crime about 100 metres by 200 metres, much of which is up to your ankles in mud and water, and involving 25 corpses. So there was not a proper investigation carried out by that judge under the terms of an investigation as I understand it. In my conversation with General Loncar outside the farmhouse we exchanged a number of comments and at the end of which I said, Let's have a joint investigation. And he said, Yes, let's have a joint investigation. I said I look forward to. It never happened. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's because you did not have a scene-of-crime officer's team that would come out on the site. I asked you something else: Did you seek from the Yugoslav authorities forensic and ballistic reports because you obviously are not familiar with the way an on-site investigation is carried out in the FRY? Did you ask for those reports to look at them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very very familiar with the way on-site investigations are carried out in the FRY. Certainly in Kosovo. People went in, looked around, took a very short time, and walked out declaring it all to be legitimate. That is not a proper investigation. You do not need to be a policeman in order to see a bad investigation. Bad is bad. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So did you seek that documentation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I did do, because there was an EU forensic team in Kosovo at the time sifting through the remains of other incidents, and I attempted to get them diverted on to this scene of crime, and that did not prove possible. They were a professional team, and it is a great pity that they were not allowed by the various authorities to come and investigate that properly. And it would have taken about four days to do a proper scene-of-crime investigation on that -- on that scene. As for ballistic evidence, if it had been available, then it should have been made available to us so that the FRY authorities could dispel the impression that we had and that we made pretty clear that this was excessive in the way that the operation which had begun as a legitimate operation but the way it had degenerated into non-judicial killing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ask who the killed policeman was? Where he was from? To which unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was identified by General Loncar as a member of the unit in the light grey coveralls that had carried out the storming. He was in the same uniform as the rest of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, from the previous two Kosovo trials and the present one, you are the only person mentioning a light grey uniform. Nobody has ever seen a light grey or any grey uniform on a police member anywhere. Are you saying that this was some sort of special police force with only one person in that kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was light grey or if it was a light grey-blue, it was a light grey tending to blue uniform. There were 25 of them in that uniform. It was a uniform uniform. They had a patch on their arm which was not one I'd seen before. It's a pity I didn't photograph it. It's a pity I didn't photograph them. But I know what I saw, and I'm still under oath. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you see how long it took you to say grey blue uniforms. Thank you. I'd like to ask you something about the information that was available to you concerning the activity of the Kosovo Liberation Army in the area of Kacanik and their relationship with the civilians. Do you recall what it was that was going on towards the end of February and what kind of information and reports you had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you share it with us?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Towards the end of February, the area in the extreme south of Kosovo, an area which up until this point had not had any noticeable KLA presence in the area, started to see KLA activity. As a result of this, the FRY forces carried out an operation in that area in which they surrounded the area and dealt with the KLA. I understand the sensitivity of the area to the FRY authorities because it -- that high ground dominated the main road between Pristina and Skopje. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any reports that these were members of the KLA who had arrived from Macedonia and the commander leading them was not a local, he was not from that area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, we thought they had moved from elsewhere within Kosovo but we did not get the impression that they were indigenous to the Kacanik area certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you have the information that they were abusing civilians, forcing them to leave their villages to stay in the woods in order to portray that as a humanitarian catastrophe for journalists who arrived and spread it all over the world as KLA propaganda?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard rumours to that effect, not necessarily at the time. However, when we went up on to the plateau and we looked it at the areas where fighting had taken place, we were -- we did note that in the villages where fighting had taken place, only a small number of houses had been burned. And this was reported to us by the FRY authorities, that only those houses where KLA had actually been occupying were burned, and the rest were left standing. In the next few days, those villages completely burned, and we did suspect that the KLA were burning those villages in order to attempt to put the blame on to the FRY. We reported that these operations in the Kacanik area were noted as being less violent than the other ones we had seen previously. And I remember this led the NATO Secretary-General, when he saw these reports, to comment only -- only devastating one village per day keeps NATO away, in other words, keeping the level of violence down at that low level was ensuring that NATO would not use its Activation Order. So that was a comment also on the fact that this operation was more restrained by the FRY forces than others that we had seen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I read to you that it "... appeared as if over 100 KLA members crossed the border and clashed with the aforesaid police," does that remind you of reports from end February and beginning of March, reports by the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see my learned colleague is reading from a document. If he could, I don't know, tell us the source of the document, put it on the screen for the witness so he can properly assess what's in the document and comment on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your reference, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but to the best of my understanding, if I put a question and the witness confirms, I'm not obliged to show the document. This is 680 on the 65 ter list. It's an OSCE report for the period from the 26th of February to the 4th of March. I'm using portions of it to remind the witness. If the witness says yes, I move on without wasting time, provided he confirms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your understanding is not complete or accurate, I'm afraid, Mr. Djurdjic. If you are quoting a document to the witness, you will need to identify it. If you are asking the witness whether it is true that on a certain date 20 houses were burned in the village of so and so and he says yes, you have not referred to a document at all. Do you see the difference? When you are quoting a document at the witness, you will need to identify it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In this report for the 26th of February until the 4th of March -- I'll read out: "The most significant activity of the KLA was on the forward location of Djeneral Jankovic, in this area" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: "It was quiet here the week before, before the activity started." "It was quiet in this area before fighting started this week."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we will need to have the document on the screen if you are going into this detail from a particular document, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I attempt to help?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this report is looking back. It's a weekly report, so it was written after what had happened had happened by several days. And I think that we got this information that KLA from or people, fighters from Macedonia, had crossed the border into Djeneral Jankovic and they had not -- not moved within Kosovo to Djeneral Jankovic. I think we got that information some time after the operation, several days after the operation, but that's certainly -- that's where I think I got that from. At the time that it was happening, we did not understand that to be the case, we later, a few days later found out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told the report is already in evidence, Mr. Djurdjic. D157. And the first page is now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, it goes on to say: "By encouraging the movement of IDPs (internally displaced persons) the international media was able to claim a Serb offensive was underway."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm looking for that. Right, yes. That was clearly what we thought at the time. We had a lot of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You see the beginning of the page where it says: "... there is a significant movement of the KLA from Macedonia." The last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Owing to the belief that there was a substantial KLA movement from Macedonia. So the report that we sent up to Vienna said that it was the belief, not the fact. Now, it may well have been the fact, but the piece of paper we are referring to refers to a belief. That's an impression. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about the next paragraph: "The KLA force in the Podujevo area managed to carry out an attack in the town itself - effectively taking the fight to the Serbs..."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this demonstrates that even at the end of February and the beginning of March, this mission that I was in was still attempting to be evenhanded in its judgement of the parties to the conflict. Where the KLA clearly acted in a way that was inappropriate, we reported it. Should we not have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, at that time -- in fact, does this document reflect your contemporaneous knowledge? It seems the KLA entered the region with 120 to 160 men, the KLA told villagers in the area to move out. Almost all of them left their homes by the 28th February leading to an IDP report on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's clearly the situation as we understood it a few days later, because this is a -- again, I think this is part of a weekly report. So this is with the benefit of hindsight, not necessarily what we knew at the moment that it was happening. But I'm happy that that's what we reported, and that was the information as we understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get page 5 in B/C/S, please. Sorry, English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, it says here in a subheading: "KLA ..." -- the subheading is assessment. "KLA: Exploiting the media. In recognising the power of the media, the ethnic Albanians will continue to work on international sympathy for their cause. The plight of the IDP remains their strongest weapon..." And towards the bottom four lines down it says: "It should be remembered that ethnic Albanians watch Albanian television and such a medium could well be used in conjunction with other methods to increase the propaganda effort."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were absolutely fully aware that the international media were not impartial in this, and that was why we were making these points to Vienna. Because up in Vienna was a -- a large gathering of international diplomats who, as well as getting our reports, were watching the international media every day. And we needed to make the point that the international media were in our view being manipulated, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to come back to the organisation of the KVM. Would it be fair to say that it was perhaps not identical but basically identical in terms of the organisation of the headquarters, regional centres, and local centres; they had a liaison officer for the army, liaison for the police, liaison officer for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the greatest extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me, at the level of the KVM headquarters, who were the liaison officers for the KLA, if you still remember?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they varied with time, but the first one that I recall getting into them was -- was someone called David Wilson. And then I detached in the middle of the night my military assistant David Meyer because we were literally phoned up out of the blue and told that if we wanted to meet the KLA leadership, we should get someone to a certain crossroads within an hour and a half. And this was at 10.30 at night. I only had one person with me, I sent him. Various other people acted as liaison with the KLA, but David Meyer became my principal link to them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the level of regional centres and especially coordination centres, how did these liaison officers for the KLA work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one of three ways: In some cases they stayed with them for some time; in other cases they routinely visited them; and they were in contact by mobile phone for the rest of the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: These mobile phones were actually satellite phones; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. We did not, to the best of my knowledge, ever provide the KLA with phones. We did use satellite phones sometimes in areas where there was no mobile phone coverage, for the obvious reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I didn't say that it was you who gave them satellite phones. I meant to say or ask you did your officers have satellite phones in order to communicate with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because you couldn't use mobile phones in many areas. There was no coverage. And the radio didn't cover in all the areas because there were two many hills in the way, so you had to use satellite phones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, after you left Kosova-Metohija, what was the function of these KLA liaison officers in Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed in touch with their counterparts in the KLA to the greatest extent possible in order to remain aware of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And they were the source of the your information, in fact; am I right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were one of many sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the FRY army liaison officers, what role did they assume after you had left?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attempted to remain in contact with them, but they turned their phones off when we attempted to phone them up, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. But these officers who were in charge of liaising with the FRY, what did they do after you went to Macedonia? Were they assigned some other duties? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once it was clear that the liaison, their counterparts had turned their phones off, I put them on to other duties, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After crossing into Albania and Macedonia, did you have liaison officers for NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Liaison is a function. You exchange liaison officers with all the people with whom you deal so that there is an unfettered exchange of information. That's what liaison officers do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what kind of connections did you have with NATO during the war? What was your relationship with NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a close one. We worked hands in hand with them as far as the humanitarian crisis was concerned. For instance, the Brezda camp was entirely built but NATO soldiers. We assisted in that -- in that project as assistance to the UNHCR. There was a meeting between Walker and the lady in charge of UNHCR who came down from Geneva, at which they agreed that we should act in support of UNHCR while the refugee crisis was ongoing. So there was a very strong link with UNHCR and there was a less strong link with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And all this relationship was to do solely with humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else are you asking me? I mean, I can remember that the amount of work we put into humanitarian issues. What else are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D1011, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is, as you explained, a document that you used at the press conference. Can you tell me, this press conference held at Whitehall was intended for journalists and reporters; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Here in paragraph 3 you say as follows: "As you know, we were ordered out 12 days ago. Since then we have remained in contact with the KLA..."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And this is what you said at the press conference, that you were still in contact with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in the next paragraph you said that air campaign is having positive effects on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the positive side we have had confirmation that the air campaign is having some effect on the ground." What that, I think, I should interpret that as the air campaign is reducing the ability of the Serbian forces to attack civilians, Albanian civilians. That's what it was doing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And that was the KVM mission in Macedonia at the time, for you to assess how successful the NATO bombing was; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were receiving reports that the NATO bombing was de-appetizing the FRY forces in their attempt to -- or in their endeavours to attack unarmed Albanian civilians. The way to avoid being bombed by NATO was to stop attacking unarmed Albanian civilians. NATO aircraft attacking FRY forces is a more legitimate activity then FRY forces attacking unarmed civilians. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Cluster bombs and depleted Uranium bombs constitute also a proper and proportionate use of force; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, luckily the KVM's duties didn't involve loading the ammunition on to the planes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Apparently you would have done that gladly. Can you tell me, what capacity did you hold this press conference in Whitehall in London?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the KVM who was in London for consultation with his government. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you obtain an approval from Vienna for this press conference to be held in Whitehall by you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall I did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to you, Witness, for stating my personal opinion concerning what you mentioned about loading the planes. You just provoked me into making this comment, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at document 1027, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, this is your preparatory document that you had. In this second part where you say a 35-year-old OSCE official, it is not possible to establish the identity of this source because it's not specified here which particular official told you this.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this would have been one of our locally employed civilians, a Kosovar Albanian. We wouldn't have identified him by name in this. It would have been inappropriate. It would have put his family at risk no doubt. But this would have been a report which we received again by mobile phone talking to people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of this document, you say that the KLA is deploying the resources for offensive activities against the Serbian targets --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the counsel please be more specific about the portion that he is reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: "And the protection of its own displaced population."

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the note said. That was the view of the people who had been talking to the KLA by phone on what the position of the KLA was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But if we put this in the context of the document that we looked at referring to the period between the end of February and beginning of March, that the Albanians were interested in propaganda effects and providing justification for an attack on the FRY, and that for that purpose they forced their population on the move in order to achieve these effects, were you not giving this any consideration at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we obviously were taking these reports and checking them to the greatest extent possible, but I don't think we should equate what we were reporting at the end of February when we were in country attempting to be evenhanded with the situation 12 days after we had been ordered out. And during those 12 days there had been, in our views, uncontrovertible evidence of a major assault by all of the available sources of FRY, including units that had come in from outside on the civilian population of Kosovo. That was entirely outwith every one of the deals that we had gone in. So the agreement really just wasn't there anymore. There was no agreement. If there was an agreement, then presumably all of this bombing and driving out of the Albanian civilians during late March and April was done from three company positions and 27 police posts, only nine of which were ever occupied. I don't think so. So this is a completely different situation. This is a situation in which entirely illegitimate activity is taking place by the forces of FRY and that's why they are being bombed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, before the bombing started, there were no refugees or maybe not more than 1.000 prior to the 24th of March, and all your sources are Albanian sources?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you know there were no more than 1.000 prior to the 24th of March? Were you there? Did you count them? No you did not. I do not accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm only looking at your document. My only source of information are your documents.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Let me talk to you about the numbers of refugees then. We found it very difficult to work out exactly how many people had been displaced, and we were very very keen not to support wild figures which we felt were being given by some sectors of the media. And, therefore, we went out looking for them and where we could find them, we reported them. It was our view that when a village was emptied, that the people that fled the village would take refuge with relatives as soon as they could because that was natural. And so if they had a relative in the next village, they would go and live in the next village. Now, that still made them IDPs, but it meant that we didn't count them because we would try to find out where the clusters of IDPs were, and we never found more than a few hundred. But were people displaced from their villages? Yes, they were. Because of the nature of Albanian society, they have a lot of relatives in surrounding villages, and so they went and took refuge with them. That's our understanding of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit D151.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, does the name Atrim Aziri ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Afrim Aziri.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how did you make his acquaintance and what kind of contacts you had with him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early on in the mission, he drove me on a number of occasions. When we got a greater number of people, I got somebody else to drive me. I remained -- he remained someone that I was aware of and if I saw him I would chat to him and exchange the time of day with him. He occasionally, when I was going to meetings, drove the vehicle with the interpreters in it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to his statement, he continued to work for the KVM after your departure for Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true. He turned up in Macedonia. He made his own way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He stated that he was in contact with KLM [as interpreted] commanders who were feeding him information about the Serbian forces in Kosovo, their numbers, the weapons that they had, and the deployment areas. Sir, were you aware of these contacts of his?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that he was one of the people we used to talk to the KLA, yes. One of a number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He goes on to say that initially this information was being collected for the OSCE HQ. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the information he was collecting was part of the contacts that -- the results of the contacts that we were having by mobile phone to try to find out what was going on on the ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He also says that: "Richard Ciaglinski and David Meyer discussed this information with me and suggested that it might probably be shared with the NATO command. I agreed that this should be done." Tell me, sir, at the time, was Colonel Ciaglinski at the time a liaison officer for NATO in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thanks. And Mr. David Mayer was a liaison officer for the KLM [as interpreted] while you were in Kosovo-Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And he remained in contact with the KLA when we were in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that a letter from the Supreme Command of the KLA was forwarded through this gentleman to General Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We acted as a post box so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall Mr. Agim Musliu?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as such. Can you help me with a few clues?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. He was a security advisor for the KVM headquarters in Pristina during your stay in Kosovo and Metohija, and that he used to accompany you to visit KLA locations and crime scene investigations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was either -- he may have been an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You don't remember. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit D004-1283.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This document contain a lot of protest letters concerning the border crossing regimes and similar affairs. What you are going to see is the protest letter issued by the government of the FRY concerning an incident which took on the 26th and 27th February and the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing. It's been mentioned a few times in these documents. I wanted to ask you the following: Were you familiar with the procedure that should have been followed in compliance with the Vienna Convention and applied at border crossings by people and vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was generally aware that we had diplomatic immunity and therefore our vehicles were not required to be opened for inspection. And I think this incident was one at which the border guards exceeded their authority and detained a number of KVM vehicles and their occupants at the border for up to 24 hours because they required that the back of a vehicle be opened in defiance of the Vienna Convention. Eventually, Ambassador Walker turned up and directed that in order to finish this incident, that despite the requirement not to open the backs of vehicles, he directed that the back of the vehicle should be opened in order to get the quite large number of people of the KVM who were all held at this border, in effect being held hostage against their will by the FRY authorities, he directed that the back be opened. I think that's the incident you are talking about. It was a disgrace.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, according to the Vienna Convention there are certain rules that are applicable even to persons who enjoy diplomatic immunity. This protest which was handed over to the Kosovo Verification Mission, it says that the containers that entered did not have any diplomatic insignia, that the content was not properly declared in accordance with the Vienna Convention, and that it contained such items and equipment that according to the Vienna Convention have to be declared. And then they say one optical sight, a pistol, a holster, equipment, medical and chemical substances, and other commodities that are bound to be declared. Then it goes on to say that two vehicles contained only FRY staff, local staff, without any members of the mission present. Therefore, due to these reasons an official protest was submitted and forwarded to the mission on the 24th of February.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what's your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this procedure, border crossing procedure, owing to which your vehicles were halted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is the first vehicle to be halted was my vehicle coming back from Skopje with one of my drivers in it who had just dropped me off at the airport. Other vehicles then were impounded. And if some of them had local staff in without a KVM official, then clearly that's reprehensible; and I'm sure that it could have been dealt with without holding people there for 24 hours, and holding them in effect at gun point. It's proportionality, I think, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I'm talking about the customs border organs, I'm not talking about army and the police. They are a separate service. And they say that certain things were either not declared or improperly declared and were disallowed even under the Vienna Convention. I'm asking you if you were aware about this protest lodged with you about the incident that took place on the 25th and 26th February, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I am aware. I ended up in this farrago, because when I got back from wherever I had been going to, I found that my number one car was still at the border. So I ended up in this. I think we also wrote a protest. Have you got that available?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No. I haven't seen any of your protest letters in evidence, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a good time, Your Honours, for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd forgotten towards the end of the last session, can we please admit D004-1283 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which one is that, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's this last document we looked at, the protest of the FRY to the KVM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00228.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please be seated, General. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you assist me with this, the acronym AARC [as interpreted], what does it mean in some of the reports I've seen, the KVM reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ARRC is a the Ace Rapid Reaction Corps which was the headquarters which became headquarters KFOR. Because KFOR had no legal standing at this time, it had to remain calling itself what it called itself in peacetime, namely the headquarters of the Ace Rapid Reaction Corps a NATO formation based in Rheindahlen and commanded by General Mike Jackson. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about S-I-T-C-E-N?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sitcen would be a situation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Whose situation centre? Which organisation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every military organisation and most peacekeeping organisations have a situation centre. That's what we call the operations room. But it could be called the situation centre. It's the place to which all reports come. It's the place which I described yesterday was run by my good friend the retired German colonel Ilez [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And there's one other acronym, S-H-A-P-E?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the military headquarters of NATO based in Mons commanded by Sakija [phoen] called Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe. It's also referred to as superb holidays at public expense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did you know Clark Christopher John?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Clark was a British officer, also an engineer, and he was together with you in the KVM in 1998/1999 in Kosovo-Metohija; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a warrant officer. That means he was not a commissioned officer. He was a technician who had served about 20 years in the army, in the ranks. But, yes, he was with me in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that over time he established contact with the KLA while working for the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. His principal duties were to advise me on any bomb incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably also not allowable under the Vienna Convention, advising me on bomb incidents. Shall I tell you about the day that he defused an improvised explosive device with a pen knife? That was probably not in accordance with the Vienna Convention either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, these things happened on the ground and he was an expert. I believe he mentioned it in his evidence, but we'll come to that later. In the course of February and March 1999, he was in the area of Kacanik and Kotlina, and he informed both you and the KVM that members of the KLA had been infiltrated from Macedonia and the leader of that newly come unit was a man with a pseudonym Bardhi. Do you remember him reporting to you about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I don't dispute that that may well have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And he goes on to say that the KLA ordered the local Albanian population to leave the area and forced them to cross the border and go to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then he says that in the operative zone Dukadjini there was an international unit made up of men from various countries who are not Kosovo Albanians and that this was information widely available.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then you don't need me to confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think you also said yourself that in certain areas members of the KLA wore uniforms while in other ares they were in civilian clothes or combined civilian clothes with parts of uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The problem in this area is that so do most of the workmen working on building sites. If you go anywhere in this area, you find everybody is wearing bits of cast-off uniform because it's clothing that they have that they don't mind getting dirty when they're working on dirty jobs. So bits of uniform are readily available and worn for things like gardening. It's not a very reliable indicator, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Clark says that due to the escalation in December 1998, a large number of KLA operations began against Serb positions and there were reactions to these attacks and that he was tasked by you to double-check reports by other verifiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to object to the form my learned colleague is using to question this witness. He is putting some information given by Mr. Clark. Mr. Clark is not a witness in this case. The evidence of Mr. Clark is not before Your Honours, and if my learned colleague wants to lead evidence of Mr. Clark, he can call him as a witness, but I don't believe this is an appropriate way to question the witness on these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think we could uphold your objection in its present form. The difficulty with the way Mr. Djurdjic is proceeding, though, has other fronts. If the witness is able to confirm something you put to him as being the fact or something within his knowledge, that's fine. But otherwise, nothing is being gained by it being or not being something that Mr. Clark or somebody other has said at some other time. It's not evidence before us. So perhaps you could become clearer in your own mind and then in your own questions why it's relevant to put to the witness that this is something Mr. Clark has said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm happy to confirm that Mr. Clark was one of several people that I used to go and check on the veracity of reports because I was extremely keen that the reports that we sent up the line were as good as they could be. And when we were dealing with a lot of people who were verifiers who barely spoke English, it was important to make sure what ground truth really looked like. So I used a small number of people who worked direct to me to go and check if I felt there was doubt and it was a really important incident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, were you aware that verifiers from US KDOM were biased and that is why you double-checked their reports through, among other people, Mr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that not everybody was as experienced as Clark, and I can certainly recall at least one occasion where a wild report from a newly arrived US verifier suddenly found itself on the desk of General Clark, the supreme allied commander Europe, and this was in danger of escalating the situation to a ridiculous extent before we had ascertained what actually happened. And so on that occasion, I think not only Clark but myself went to the scene. We checked with the verifier what he thought had been said to him. We checked with the VJ sentry what the sentry thought he had said. Clearly there was a misunderstanding because the sentry didn't speak English and the US KDOM member didn't speak Serbian. As a result of that, I personally phoned General Clark and put the matter to rest. That's the extent to which we would go to try to prevent misunderstanding and to try to prevent the situation from escalating. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in all villages with KLA presence and with fighting going on there was also civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the villages where there was KLA presence were villages where the population was largely Kosovar Albanian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you informed that the operation in Racak had been planned and notified to KVM officials?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before the event, no. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. David Meyer was at Stimlje police station before the events in Racak and that on that occasion he was told that the operation would go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware, but then David Meyer wasn't MUP liaison. He may have had a conversation in which someone indicated that something was going to happen. That is not notification. Notification is when the authorised person on the MUP side speaks to the authorised person on the liaison side and says this is what's going to happen, ideally well in advance, and ideally in writing. That absolutely did not happen. A piece of loose talk in a police station between two people is not notification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you aware that the KVM had issued instructions to two patrols to be in Racak village, that these instructions were not obeyed, and these patrols remained in Stimlje contrary to the instructions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I would think at this stage there were probably in excess of 100 patrols in Kosovo and I didn't personally task each one. Furthermore, each patrol was allowed to use its own discretion in terms of where it actually stayed at any moment. So if it was in Stimlje and was told to go to Racak, I don't know why it decided not to, but Stimlje is about 2 kilometres from Racak, so it's not as though they ran away to Belgrade. They were in the area and able to report on whatever was going on there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but subsequently did you hear that these were supposed to be US KDOM patrols and that great suspicions arose why exactly they were unwilling to obey the instructions they had received from the KVM?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Round about this time we had not fully absorbed all of the US KDOM, and they were still operating semi-independently. So if they were ordered by us, I think it's probably a case that they were invited by us to go to a particular place, not least because Racak was not part of the area we were covering at that moment. We were covering an area who straight line went about 2 kilometres west of Racak. So it's possible that that was why they were there. And as I say, they were operating at that stage under a different chain of command, which wasn't 100 per cent under my control. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did you trust Mr. Clark and his reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes, within the limits of his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With your leave, General, I'd like to move now to a different issue. You have attained the highest degree of education in the military, both in terms of strategy and tactics. I'd like to know your opinion about KLA activity in end December and January in the territory of Podujevo, Kosovska Mitrovica, and Vucitrn. Strategically speaking, what was your conclusion why these KLA operations were launched?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were attempting to provoke the FRY forces into reacting to them in the knowledge that any reaction was likely to be overreaction and would be self-defeating for the FRY authorities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the road from Prokuplje via Podujevo to Pristina is the most important land communication line that connects Kosovo and Metohija with the rest of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are also familiar with railroads. Would cutting off the railway near Kosovska Mitrovica and another railroad through Kosovska Mitrovica cut off all supplies from Serbia towards Pristina and further south?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would if it was used, but that railroad was hardly used south of Mitrovica. I remember we did a report on how to get the railroad working again. We wouldn't have done a report on how to get the railway working again, if the railway had been working. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if both roads are cut off both via Vucitrn and via Kosovska Mitrovica, then you cannot transport equipment and weapons even up to there; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why would you want to transport vehicles and weapons up to there? You had all the weapons and vehicles in Kosovo that were -- that were allegedly there prior to October. If you had wanted to bring anything in, it would have been in violation of the agreement. So it's an entirely academic question, I put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Academically speaking, I read the newspapers and I saw that NATO was threatening a ground invasion. Was Serbia allowed to prepare to defend itself from the invasion, or was it supposed to just sit there and do nothing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, in February and early March of 1999, Serbia was perfectly capable of preparing the area in the south of Kosovo against any NATO invasion. They prepared the tunnels for demolition with explosives and they prepared the bridges for demolition with explosives, and as an engineer, I know what that looks like. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's natural. I agree with you it's natural to prepare a defence for an upcoming attack. Therefore, you believe that these attacks and provocations by the KLA did not include the cut-off of these main communications. Do you remember that in February Mr. Walker as head of mission had a meeting on the 12th of February with Mr. Leonid Ivasov.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who precisely was Mr. Leonid Ivasov.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He was a Russian army general and he was with the defence ministry of Russia at the time. Have you heard at all about this meeting between Mr. Walker and Mr. Ivasov in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I didn't. I'm surprised he didn't take me with him, but no. And this is the first I have heard of it. A rare occurrence on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, things always happen for the first time. But in principle, were you aware of the objections of Russia to Mr. Walker's work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Walker had a Russian deputy who was permanently located in the -- in Pristina. And he was perfectly able to convey instructions from his government because that was one of the things that the various deputies did. I actually recall the relationship between Walker and the Russian deputy as being rather better than I had expected, and certainly his relationship with his Russian deputy was not the worst relationship he had with any deputy. It was a professional relationship in which there were differences, but they understood that both had differences as to the exact way in which the mission was to work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I perceive you as an international OSCE mission although you said this was a mixed intragovernmental commission. But regardless of that, that there are certain disagreements professionally, I even remember a meeting where you made some decisions, but we will come to that if we have time. But I'm talking about Russia's position and their objections to Mr. Walker's work. Irrespective how this internal organisation worked. There was an impression that not all the opinions of all verifiers were being taken into account, and I'm referring here to the Russian verifiers, Swedish verifiers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't possible for the Russian verifiers to go everywhere, because the KLA occasionally stopped our patrols and said, Who's in there? And the Russians had to hide behind the back seat because they said if there's any Russians there we're going to take them out and kill them. So we made a decision based on wishing to keep the Russians alive that we wouldn't deploy Russians into KLA areas for their own safety. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that upon having found that the Russian verifiers opinions were being disregarded, that Russia forwarded this directly to Vienna HQ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of such a specific objection. I am aware that there were different opinions on how precisely we should verify and how hard we should look, yeah. There were certainly many different opinions, and this was inherent in a mission that came together so quickly and did not have time to establish proper procedures. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that, but the point here is that the reports coming from Pristina to Vienna were contrary to the reports dispatched by Russian verifiers, and for that reason, Russia decided to send these reports directly to Vienna. I mean the ones who had already been in Pristina but were sort of disregarded.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask all 1379 people of their opinion, they will all have a different opinion. Everybody came from somewhere. And it was fully understood that the Russians were more -- were more favourably inclined towards the Serbs. Some of the others were more favourably inclined towards the KLA. That's why when the reports got to the mission headquarters it was our job to put some balance on it, and that's what we tried to do. It was certainly the case that individual ambassadors in Vienna rang the individual verifiers on the ground and said, What's it look like to you? And this came to a memorable moment when I personally said to the chairman in office, Look, if you don't believe us, you come down here, and you stand down here, and get shot at; and I'll come up to Vienna and I'll be the chairman in office, and we'll see how each of us does. You have to trust the people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that there were some objections to certain members of the mission being involved in certain intelligence work which was also contrary to the mandate that they had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were concerns, and I'm being very careful because I'm not saying that anyone was involved in intelligence work that was contrary to the mandated that they had. Because I was in charge of the fusion cell, and I knew what it was doing. There were concerns in Vienna that what the fusion cell was doing looked like intelligence to the uninitiated, to people that didn't understand it. I know that 99 per cent of the information they were using and analysing - and that was their job, analysing - was open-source information. There were moments, very occasional, when we got information which was classified from other sources which directly affected the safety of members of the mission, and that was handled in a way that was appropriate to that information, and we used the information to keep the verifiers alive. Now, if that was contrary to the Vienna Convention, then perhaps getting about 20 of our guys killed would have been in accordance with the Vienna Convention; but if we had lost verifiers, the mission would have been out of Kosovo very quickly because the people in Vienna were very very windy, very concerned, very frightened, about the safety of the verifiers. So the safety of the verifiers was something that was important, and I was prepared to accept a small amount of life-saving intelligence in order to keep people alive. And when we were getting that intelligence, it was handled by the people that were authorised to use it. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I am not talking about intelligence -- security related intelligence information, I'm talking about intelligence information about the FRY forces that were made available to certain countries and NATO members which was contrary to the mandate and that this criticism and objection forwarded to Vienna focused on this. And also, if we remember that army barracks were photographed. Can you tell me, was that also part of the KVM mandate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing in the KVM mandate that said we couldn't use cameras; and if I had been able to use a camera at Rogovo, we wouldn't have all this nonsense about whether or not these guys in grey or blue uniforms existed. So, yes, photographing stuff was part of our mandate. Nobody told us not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the army barracks, not about the incident in Rogovo where you were invited. I wonder where these photographs of the barracks ended up and the pictures of the equipment that was inside the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you will recall we were called the Verification Mission and one of the things we had to verify was where the units were. And one of the ways of doing that was to photograph what was inside the barracks so that we could ascertain what was inside the barracks as well as what was outside the barracks. And if you photograph the equipment that is on the barracks square on day 1 and you photograph it a few days later and you compare the two and you discover that on day 1 there are 40 armoured vehicles there and on day 20 there are only 6 armoured vehicles there then you wonder where the remainder have gone.
