It's quite a good way of checking against time that the situation has not changed. And that's what we were there for. So it was entirely appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And where have these photographs ended up?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I think my back would have broken if I had hauled any more stuff out of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware that a regiment for special tasks from the UK was transferred before the aggression to the territory of Macedonia and that eight intelligence units were established?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 80.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You really are going to get me sent to jail, this is absolutely straight in the face of my Official Secrets Act. I cannot discuss what our Special Forces and military intelligence units were doing at the time. You have to not question me on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Am I allowed to ask any questions about the Americans?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were in the NATO alliance in the same operation. I'm here to talk about what I saw as a member of the Kosovo Verification Mission, not the rumour that went around the bars in Skopje. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that you had close cooperation with NATO up to 20th of March, and especially after the 24th of March, and that you exchanged more than information with them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Up to the 20th of March it was extremely important that they knew exactly where we all were inside Kosovo because there was at least a reasonable chance that instead of being allowed out of Kosovo, some or all of us could have been detained and held hostage in order to stave off NATO bombing. We were very aware of this. If that took place, it was important that the people that were going to have to come and get us out knew where we were and how many of us there were in those locations. So it was part of our insurance policy in case such action took place and of course such action had taken place earlier in Bosnia in 1995. And so this was not speculation on our part, this was prudent activity on our part. After the 20th of March, again we spoke at length with NATO about the locations that they were likely to be going into, because it was quite clear that they were going to go into Kosovo eventually, and when they went into Kosovo, we were able to help them describing the sort of places that would be sensible for them to set up so that they could set up quickly in order to quickly get on top of the situation so that any law and order vacuum was avoided to the greatest extent possible. That was why we even, in, I think late February or early March, sent a team of KVM people up to the Ace Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters in Rheindahlen to brief them on that sort of thing. So before the bombing started, we were already doing that, and we were doing that in order to assist the efforts of the international community in the case of a successful end to the Rambouillet negotiations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, were you aware that the KLA had RPG-7?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were you aware that they had guns whose range was between 3 and 4 kilometres, and that they also had various calibre mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them came from Albania when the armouries were looted in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that they had Howitzers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never saw any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, do you know that KLA members, when this Racak incident happened, had been using mortars -- had used mortars on the 15th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically off the top of my head, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were, if I'm not wrong, in Racak on the 16th of January together with Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And you were also in the company of the KLA commander who was in Racak at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet him. Walker did, I think, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Walker went to a meeting in the mosque at which he said to me, as I recall it, that he met the head man of the village. There were KLA in the village at some stage that we were there, but I did not meet anybody who claimed to be a commander, and I did not see anybody going around who appeared by his actions to be a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that on the 15th of January, the KLA opened fire from mortars?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. I'm not sure where this is leading because whatever happened was not, in my view, in any way appropriate to the non-judicial killing of over 40 people. And I think that's what I'm giving evidence about. About disproportionality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you are offering here your opinions and conclusions. However, I want only to establish whether you knew about certain facts or not, and it is up to the honourable Chamber to draw conclusions and decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at Exhibit D004-0101, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm going to need the English. My Serb is not that good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, you are the best non-speaking -- non-B/C/S speaking witness in terms of your command of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I keep coming back here, I'm going to become even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You are welcome to come. Sir, this is a record that the foreign ministry compiled in Pristina about a meeting between Colonel Orsini and Lieutenant-Colonel Ciaglinski with Mr. Loncar. But this is just leading me to another question, because attached to this document, the issue of the movement of KVM members was raised. I don't know if you were ever informed by Mr. Ciaglinski that there were any discussions about the movement of KVM verifiers concerning fighting between the KLA and the FRY forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by this stage, I mean, this is the 15th of March, this is five days before we drive out. By this stage our freedom of movement was very very severely constrained by the FRY forces. And so whatever the discussions were, I am sure that they related to the fact that we were being stopped from going where we needed to go in the execution of our duties, and told that we could go no further, and therefore all we could do was speculate about what was happening on the other side of the roadblock. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, the government of the FRY was principally responsible under all agreements for your safety and security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but we found that this was used as a convenient excuse for preventing us from going to where we needed to go when it suited the people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now, can we please first look at item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You can see here there were negotiations being held to the effect to have the verifiers sign a statement that they were entering the fighting areas at their own risks and that they were to be responsible for the consequences of anything -- or of coming to any harm. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that proposal was made by us in order to get around the use of the issue of the concern for the safety of the verifiers that was being -- that was being used as the excuse for not letting us through. I have to say that the ability of the FRY forces to keep our verifiers safe was sometimes in question. I recall MUP dragging a couple of my verifiers out of their vehicle and beating them up one day up by Podujevo, so there were a moments when we were a bit skeptical about this sacred duty that the FRY forces had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, is this the proposed form of the statement to be signed by your verifiers when entering fighting zones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was, I think, our proposal which we were doing under considerable protest because we believed the whole thing to be a ruse to deny us access. We did not feel that it was any -- it was -- we felt that it was our own business. The extent to which we interpreted our freedom of movement under the agreement. And the agreement did not appear to say anywhere that we could be prevented from going anywhere for our own safety by someone who was not a member of the KVM. So this was an offer in order to keep the process going and to keep dialogue alive. It was not done by us because we wanted to do it, it was done to get around the attempt to constrain our activities still further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We extensively discussed the security of verifiers. Now, what would have been the consequences had any of the verifiers were to lose their lives in light of the FRY's obligation and responsibility to provide the protection for you because they had the highest responsibility for that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, it would have been very serious, and that was my job. To make sure that the verifiers understood that when they went forward, they knew what they were doing. My problem was actually the other way around. There were quite a lot of verifiers that we found standing two hills back complaining that their binoculars weren't strong enough and at that point I was having to take them by the hand and take them forward a couple of hills and show that if they went forward a bit they didn't need such strong binoculars. So our problem was to get them to go forward in many cases rather than to protect them from the consequences of their actions. Thank you. And that sort of explains why we needed binoculars and telescopes in the back of vehicles, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00229.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, do you know that Mr. Gilbertson and Ed Sullivan as well as Mr. Giovanni Santini attended the crime scene investigation in Racak on the 18th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I know that Gilbertson was the deputy head of that regional centre that covered that area, so that would have not been a surprise to me. I probably knew it at the time but have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Jan Robert Hendry and Mark Pederson were present during the autopsy of the bodies found in Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lot of people were present at the autopsies of the bodies found in Racak because it went on for a very long time, so they may well have been among the people. By the time they got to the autopsy, these bodies were in a very advanced state of decay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you this: Did General Maisonneuve inform you about his meeting with the commander of the operation zone Drini and that the latter had informed him that certain KLA members who were seriously injured in Racak were still in hospital, whereas others had been discharged from hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Maisonneuve met Drini from time to time, and it is possible that Maisonneuve did inform me that KLA members were injured in the Racak operation, which is, I think, what you're telling me. Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let me ask you this, a short while ago you describe today me the procedure of crime scene investigation. Now, when on 16th of January, 1999, you and Mr. Walker arrived at Racak, did your verifiers after you arrived secure the area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stop those present from tampering with the bodies in terms of moving them and doing various things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the bodies moved or tampered with at any stage when I was on the hill. If they were tampered with, they were tampered with by people over whom we had no authority. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Of course you did not have any authority over the 50 journalists who accompanied you to Racak and went whichever way they pleased. Did you notice people, however, picking up casings or other evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember people picking up shell casings, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I have another question that does not require an expert. Why did you allow any moving of the bodies if you were already there with the verifiers and you had your own experts?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not in charge of that scene. There were a small number of KVM people and a large number of media. It was not our job, and we could not have secured the crime scene; and I'm at a loss to know what you thought we could do. What was it we were supposed to do? We weren't equipped with, sort of, scene-of-crime tape. And if we had attempted to put scene-of-crime tape down anywhere, I'm sure that the MUP would have come along and told us not to. We might have put it all the way around the whole border of Kosovo, mind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, were there any representative of the FRY authorities at Racak at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You will recall, however, that when I had my meeting with General Loncar, I invited him to come with us, and he said he would. And I said, Right, we'll see you outside the OSCE building in half an hour. And half an hour later he wasn't there. We waited ten minutes, and he didn't turn up. So off we went without him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Right. But there were representatives of the KLA in Racak at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not when we arrived. We did not see any KLA when we arrived in the village. We were taken by villagers up the hill, and when we came back from the hill, there were KLA around on the streets. Where they had come from, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Walker perhaps inform you that the KLA commander had told him that on the 15th, at 1700 hours the KLA took control of Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in so many words. Perhaps you better talk to Mr. Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware that the investigating judge was able to come into Racak only on the 18th of January to perform the on-site investigation to the best of her ability, and that she had to pull out because she was under attack?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well, because I offered to take her into Racak myself the day before, but she declined. She didn't want to be seen with such a disreputable person as me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in the UK, would an investigating judge come into Belfast without any British security detail?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just two more short questions. Do you know that Mr. Walker attended a meeting with the General Clark, General Naumann, Mr. Kusner [phoen], and some other NATO generals when the decision was made to go forward with air-strikes against the FRY?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I am afraid to get this wrong, it could have been the 17th of March or perhaps a day earlier in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I am sure that in making the decision on the way ahead that Walker's opinion was sought as the head of the mission that was on the ground. So it wouldn't have been impossible. I can't remember precisely where he was on a day-by-day basis. He was certainly back with us when we drove out on the 20th. I have a picture of him and me stepping over the border together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One last question. Would you agree, General, that the objective of the ruling political forces in the international community at the time was to install NATO forces in Kosovo by fair means or foul?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. We went into Kosovo as the Kosovo Verification Mission genuinely determined to do our utmost to prevent NATO bombing. I promise you that. Everybody I spoke to understood that's what we were there for. And that was why that mission was put together at huge expense and with so many people. The fact that we did not manage to prevent the bombing was in no account the fault of that mission or of the selfless devotion of the people that were on it. The problem lied entirely with the FRY government, I'm afraid. It was entirely avoidable. And it's a tragedy for the Yugoslav people, for the Serb people, that that wreckless series of circumstances took place and led to the tragedy that we have seen. So I'm deeply sorry, but I do not believe that it was the intention of the international community to precipitate that bombing. It was -- the KVM was the last-chance saloon for the officials in Belgrade, and it's a huge pity that they didn't understand they had the ability to step back from this cycle of escalation at any stage, even up to Rambouillet when they could have signed the deal and we could have avoided all this. So that's my view. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I did not mean it was the intention of the KVM. But this is really my last question: Have you heard that Mrs. Madeleine Albright had told Mr. Hashim Thaqi to sign the Rambouillet agreement, and if he did she guaranteed to him a referendum on independence within three years; just give me a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this question. It's completely outside the scope of the knowledge of the witness, and it just calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to suggest this witness has any personal knowledge, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in Rambouillet, I was in Pristina at the time. Obviously we received reports of what was going on at Pristina, but again, talk to Madeleine Albright, talk to Hashim Thaqi. Get firsthand evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's your answer, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. A no would have sufficed. Thank you very much, General. Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour but I'm going to try to be as brief as possible. Could we please have Exhibit P836 up on the screen again

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, this morning you were asked a number of questions in relation to the agreement known as the Shaun Byrnes-Djordjevic Agreement, and I would just like to clarify some of your answers in this respect. And if we first look at the first paragraph of the agreement, which refers to all check-points will be dismantled then there is a provision regarding the 27 observation points and the number that is allowed, which you've given evidence on. First of all, with regard to the first sentence about the check-points being dismantled by the MUP, this requirement. Do you have any information as to why this provision was included in the agreement? And I'm referring to this situation on the ground. Why was that required, the dismantling of all check-points by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the check-points were used as a way of harassing the local population, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, we see that the agreement does authorise the establishment of observation points and one-third of them being manned initially. Is a check-point and an observation point the same thing, or they different things?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not the same thing. An observation point is a location from which you can see what's going on on the road but it's away from the road, so it's a passive fixture. A check-point is on the road, everything that drives up or down the road has to stop and then the occupants of the vehicle do whatever they are told by the people manning the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 2, which was where you were also questioned about this paragraph by my learned colleague and it says that: "In case of incidents or increased tension, the police will have the right upon notifying KVM OSCE to perform patrol duties." Before we move to the second part of that paragraph, was this requirement of notification complied with?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In almost all cases, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, if we move to the second part of the paragraph, it says: "To perform patrol duties in armoured vehicles equipped with machine-guns of 7.9 millimetres," and I'm interested in the last part which says, "which will be used exclusively in self-defence and with restraint." Was that part of this provision to the best of your knowledge complied with when these patrol duties were carried out?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hesitating because I'm trying to remember moments when I specifically noticed MUP machine-gun operated vehicles firing as opposed to other vehicles. And I can't instantly remember one specific incident, but it is my recollection that generally when there was a fire fight going on, the MUP and the VJ fired with everything they had without restraint and certainly not exclusively in self-defence. So I can't recall any moments when machine-guns were used exclusively in self-defence and with restraint. The problem with a machine-gun is that it's belt fed, it's very difficult to use it with restraint.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I would like to now move to a different document, and this is P844. And I would like for page 4 to be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about the verification of the observation points and specifically you were shown a report by KVM dated 6 January, 1999, which stated that you carried out a verification the previous day on the 5th of January and that not all observation points were manned. And your response to my learned colleague was that on the occasion of that verification you were able to establish that there had been a breach of the agreement. This is page 5 line 9 of today's transcript. I would like you to read out the entry marked number 58 here and also if you just tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a chronology of all of my time in Kosovo which I made around about the end of April 1999, at which I tried to list everything that was of significance to us, and to put a very short comment on it, it was an aid-memoire, really, for myself. Written, as I say, just after I had left Kosovo in order to put things in chronological order in my mind. Number 58, you can read it, that all 27 OPs were inspected and most were occupied by MUP. And most is 14 or more, which is more than 9. I cannot for the life of me remember exactly how many, but it was reported to me like that. I think I was actually, on the 5th of January, I think I was coming back from three days back in England, and I think it happened on the day I came back while I was en route back. And it was Mike Maisonneuve who actually supervised all of this acting on my behalf in my absence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And you told us today and this is on page 6, that when you established that the disprovision regarding the manning of observation points had been breached, you had a meeting with General Loncar and there was a MUP representative present. Do you recall speaking about that this morning?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that 5th of January, yes, I mean, I'm sure I had a meeting probably the next day as part of getting back into the saddle and making sure that General Loncar knew I was back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did you raise this specific issue that you had carried out this verification of the observation points and that you had observed that there was a breach?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what was the reaction from General Loncar, the MUP representative present? I mean, did the situation on the ground change after you raised this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't. The retort was that this what was made necessary by the evolving deteriorating security situation on the ground, and I mean, that was -- that was credible. My point was that we should know about any decisions to go out -- to reoccupy any of these extra positions in advance so that we could then be aware of it and report on it properly and be present when it was happening. And simply to ignore us when there was an ongoing requirement to provide weekly detailed reports of MUP and VJ activity was in breach of the agreement. So it didn't matter what the justification for this was; it was in breach of the agreement because it wasn't being told to us, and we had no opportunity to discuss it with the people on the grown. That was my point. And it was the wider point of the continuing non-availability, non-provision of these detailed reports that we were supposed to get.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: After you had this meeting did the situation change regarding the provision of information about the MUP and VJ activity?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the MUP representative who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure it would have been Colonel Mijatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. My last topic. Yesterday you were shown the copy of the Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement, which is P835, and you were shown - this is page 3 paragraph 4 - which is a paragraph that refers to the border zone and the access that you had to the border zone, and specifically the provision that says the Verification Mission when invited by FRY authorities or upon its request will visit border control units. Could you explain to us if during the time you were in Kosovo you were authorised to visit border units in the border zone and how this regime worked?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were visits and inspections made to the border zone. Some were specific when there was an incident such as in December when the KLA foot convoy was ambushed, and we were invited to verify that which we did. I personally went with General Loncar's deputy, Colonel Kotur, to the border zone in February when we were trying to do the sums on what would be needed in the future on the border. The two regional centres that abutted the Albanian border, namely Pec and Prizren, had a more detailed constant interaction and dealt directly with their counterparts when they felt they needed to go into the border zone. So I don't believe that we generally went into the 5 kilometre border zone without letting the FRY authorities know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: During the time you were in Kosovo, did the border zone remain an area of 5 kilometres or was it changed in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extended to 10 kilometres by a decree in Belgrade that we were not consulted with. I don't believe the OSCE in Vienna were consulted about it, and so we regarded it as interesting but not binding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And from a military perspective does this make any difference whether the border zone is 5 or 10 kilometres? I mean, what is the importance of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would have stopped us moving up and down the main road between Pec and Prizren, for instance. I mean, yes, because -- because Kosovo is a small place, adding another 5 kilometres to the border zone, adds a very big area to the area that we would be excluded from. So it would have made our life extremely difficult. And would probably have required the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement to be renegotiated. That's the sort of effect it should have had, but of course it was early March and the whole thing was falling to pieces around us at that stage, so it was rather academic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: I have just a very short question relating to your statement of 2000. It is P996. In paragraph 23, it's on page 4, you are mentioning and describing different places of the VJ and the MUP in Pristina. You mentioned two different places where the police was stationed. Could you describe the difference between the two places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, the one that we went into was the one where the public went in to do the things that the public do in connection with the police. The sort of place where you and I would take our driving licences if we'd been caught speeding. If judges are ever caught speeding, I'm sure you are not. So that's the public place, and that was on one side of the road. And then there was another building on the other side of the road where nobody was allowed, and I have no idea what went on in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: And you had your contacts in the first building, the open-to-public building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's where our contacts came from. They tended to meet us, rather than us meet them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: General, thank you very much. You will be pleased to know that that concludes the questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance once more, for the time you've been able to spend, and the assistance you've given. And we indicate, of course, that you may now return to your normal activities. And the court officer will show you out. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will take the next break now with a view to the remaining witness commencing at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can I ask one question, Your Honour, with regard to a document that was marked for identification, well two versions of it, the Blue Book at the end of my examination-in-chief. I'm wondering if the status of this document being seen that we have completed cross-examination and my learned colleague has had the opportunity to put questions to the witness on this document, if the status of that document will change, and we would request that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is going to be considered by the Chamber during this break, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, the Chamber will indicate that it has decided that with respect to the -- what has been described as the Blue Book, that it will not change its present order in respect of the total book, but it will receive in evidence those parts of it which have been translated and which are separately in e-court at the present time. We would point out that the description "book" is in a sense misleading. It is really simply a collecting together of a series of individual daily reports and it is those reports that have been translated which we will receive. We indicate that it is done because they are reports collected by people who it was their duty to make these observations and these reports and that it is something that is acted upon by the witness who has spoken in respect of it and accepted by that organisation so that it is a matter of some propriety. We would also observe that if at any future time it is considered by counsel either for the the Defence or the Prosecution that some other parts of that book are material to their cases and should be included as an exhibit, then we will receive a motion for the addition of those additional parts. Of course that will be subject to translation of that part. And we hope by that means that if Mr. Djurdjic has not had an adequate time to consider the balance of the document, that it will be possible for him to do so and if necessary to move for the addition of any part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I'm sorry, we were dealing with another matter as you came in. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Behar has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Dedaj. Could you please begin by stating your name and your date of birth for the record?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: My name is Merita Dedaj. I was born on the 8th of January, 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ma'am, I understand that you were born in Guska in the Djakovica municipality and that you grew up in that town as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I also understand that on the 8th of April of 2000 you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor about the events that you experienced in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I understand that you also made certain corrections or clarifications to that statement on the 12th of July, 2002; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to read those statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that there's one brief correction or clarification that can be made to your initial statement. To just deal with it quickly, your statement refers to your uncle Anton Dedaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: If I can just give me friend the reference. That appears at page 4, paragraph 2, of the English; or paragraph 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, is Anton Dedaj your uncle or can you explain how you are related to him?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Anton Dedaj is my first cousin, the son of my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. With that said, are you satisfied that the information that's contained in those statements is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender those two statements. They both appear under 65 ter 02233.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01030.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Dedaj do you recall testifying at the trial of Milan Milutinovic et al. on the 10th of August, 2006?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review or to have read back to you in Albanian the transcript of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Does that transcript accurately reflect your evidence and would you testify to the same facts again today?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek to tender that transcript at 65 ter 05058.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It too will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P01031, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And I would, Your Honour, seek to tender one exhibit that was tendered in association with Ms. Dedaj's testimony in the Milutinovic case, it's Exhibit 00035. It's a map that was marked by the witness in her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P01032, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can now provide a summary of Ms. Dedaj's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Dedaj is from Guska village in the Gjakove municipality. She describes the deployment of VJ and MUP forces in her area beginning in autumn of 1998. She also describes the changes that took place in her village after the 24th of March 1999. She explains that after reportedly executing 8 civilian men --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: -- a VJ commander named Dragan came to her house on the 28th of March and told her uncles to bury those bodies, which they did. The next day at about 2.30 p.m., VJ forces led by Dragan came to Ms. Dedaj's house once again and expelled her and her family from Guska. She and her family went to Korenica and stayed there for a week. Ms. Dedaj lived in a field. From there she and her family joined a convoy of about 1.000 people. The convoy went to Meje-Orize but was then ordered back to Korenica. Ms. Dedaj and her family took shelter at a house for three weeks. On the 27th of April, 1999, Serb forces broke into that house and ordered everyone out. The women and children were separated from the men, sent out of the house, and made to yell Serbian chants. Ms. Dedaj saw the men inside being lined up by Serb forces. Among those men were her father, her uncle, and her cousin, and a number of men she knew. She heard multiple shots. And when she turned back, she saw the men falling down to the ground. She never saw those men again. Ms. Dedaj saw houses on fire and heard shooting all around. She joined a large convoy of women and children. That convoy passed Meje through Djakovica towards Prizren. In Bishtazhin police stopped the convoy at check-point and separated out more of the men. Ms. Dedaj stayed at her aunt's house in Bishtazhin along with 50 other people until NATO forces arrived in Kosovo. Five years later, the bodies of her father, uncle, and cousin were returned from mass graves in Batajnica. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Ms. Dedaj, I do have some brief questions for you in the limited time we have. You explained in your statement that on the 29th of March, 1999, Dragan returned to your house with a number of Serb forces and at that time expelled your family from Guska. And you explained that you and your family took tractors and cars and went from there to Korenica. Can you tell me, were other people from your village also expelled at that time?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. All the inhabitants of the village were expelled from the village and they went to Korenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Did you observe them being expelled and removed from the village?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: I didn't hear the order, but when we went out in the road, they too left their homes; and we formed a convoy, and all of us headed towards Korenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You described arriving in Korenica and the VJ and the police ordering you to stay in the meadow, can you explain to the Court where those VJ and police who gave you that order, where they came from? In other words, did you encounter them there or had they been with you previously?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: The forces were those of commander Dragan who came to our house and ordered us to flee. He was there with a group of the VJ and two police cars that escorted us until Korenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. You mentioned as well in your previous testimony and in your statement that you had stayed in Korenica for a week. Can I explain to the Court how and why it was that you came to leave from Korenica?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Ma'am, I understand from your statement that you stayed in Korenica for a week, and I'm wondering if you can explain why you left Korenica with that convoy at the time that you left?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: We stayed on the meadow for a week in Korenice, then the order came for us to leave Korenice and leave towards Albania. This happened one week after we were remaining on that meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And was there a time when you encountered or joined with another convoy, or was this just the same group of people that moved on from Korenica forward?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: No, there was our convoy from Guske in that meadow we stayed for a week, but people in other village, Korenice, Meje, and some other villages joined the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear, when you say in your statement that I'm quoting: "There were about 1.000 people in the convoy that moved from Korenica." That included other people who had joined from another convoy?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what ethnicity those people were amongst those 1.000 people?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You explained that the convoy went to Meje-Orize but was ordered back to Korenica, that your family then stayed in the house of Prend Markaj. I know that you've already testified about how on the 27th of April, 1999, the Serb forces broke into your house, ordered everyone out, and separated the men from the children. You described in Milutinovic - and I can give my friend the reference, this is transcript page 1413 - that when you were being forced out of the house there were no policemen there, but you said that there were policemen as well as soldiers as you were leaving, and I'm wondering if you can explain that to us, if you can clarify where it was that you saw --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just repeat that last part. I'm just wondering if you can explain to us where it was that you saw the police as you were being forced out of the house or afterward?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes. When we left the house there were police and army forces. We saw them along the way. We saw them in front of various houses in Korenice, we saw them in the meadow. Everywhere there were police and army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: So again just so that I'm clear, when you had said earlier that when you were being forced out of the house there were no policemen there but you saw them as you were leaving or after you were leaving, is that correct, were they not inside the house but outside?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Are you able to explain what those police were doing when you saw them there?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: I don't know what they were doing, but I saw them that they were armed. They were shooting all the time. As I mentioned, they were stationed in front of the various houses, along the streets, in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. You also described somewhat later in your statement being stopped at a police check-point at Bishtazhin. You explained that ten young men were separated out from the convoy at that time. You also explained that your cousin Gustin Markaj was released and that he explained to you that he was kept in a wine cellar for a number of days with other men. What I'd like to clarify with you if I could is that you say in your statement - and again the reference is at page 4, paragraph 2, or for my friend it's at paragraph 2 as well of the B/C/S - that further researches were made. And you say after those further researches at the end it was established that these men disappeared and nowadays are still missing. My question for you is if you can explain to the Court what those further researches were? In other words, how did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I myself wasn't involved in any searches, but this person, Gustin Markaj who was there with those ten males in the wine cellar, after the war was over, he asked the family members of those persons he was staying with in that cellar and from him I learned that those persons disappeared, went missing, and they are no longer found. That was what Gustin Markaj told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Those are my questions for you, and my learned friend from the Defence I expect will have some questions for you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Behar. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ms. Dedaj, my name is Veljko Djurdjic, I'm a Defence team member for the accused Vlastimir Djordjevic. First of all, let me extend my condolences for the death of your father and other of your close relatives. I didn't intend to ask you any questions, but in view of the corrections that you have made, I just wanted to ask you why did you make these corrections today regarding the police and the vehicles, and why didn't you do that in 2000 when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: I already said even before that Dragan with some soldiers came to us and ordered us to leave the house and the village within an hour. I also mentioned that there were policemen, but nobody ever asked me whether these policemen were along the way or elsewhere. But during all the time, these two police cars were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to direct your attention to your statement which says that: "On our way to Korenica we were escorted or followed by VJ vehicles." So if you look at page 3, paragraph 1 of your statement, you'll find it there.

utterances.speaker: MERITA DEDAJ
utterances.text: If you look later on, I say there that when we arrived in Korenice, the army and the police forced us to stay on that meadow. So I have said that there were police and army forces. One thing you should be clear about, when Dragan came to my house, he was accompanied with soldiers, but along the way we were escorted by these two police cars until Korenice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Dedaj, we have your statement, we have your testimony today. Thank you for your answers. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Any re-examination, Mr. Behar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Dedaj, I am pleased to be able to tell you that that completes the questioning. It had been anticipated that it might take longer. Fortunately it has been extremely quick. We would like to thank you for coming again to The Hague, for the assistance that you have been able to give, not only here today but also in your statement and your previous evidence in the Milutinovic trial. And we'll be taking all of these into account in due course. But we are happy to say that you may now return, of course, with your family to your home and carry on your normal activities. And you go with our thanks. The court officer will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to you, Your Honours. I feel honoured to have been invited to come here to tell what I went through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How many more witnesses do you think we can finish before the break? The next witness I anticipate cannot possibly be so quick. Is it feasible to spend a quarter of an hour with him, or should we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I would suggest that we adjourn, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Happy with that, Mr. Djurdjic? Well, we do not sit tomorrow or Friday at the request of the Belgrade district court before which the accused will be giving evidence, so we adjourn now to resume again on Monday and to continue the trial at that time. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
